links.note: Hethum, lord of Korikos, kept a table of the years. It says that in 1292 the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf took Hromkla, where the Armenian patriarchs lived. He seized Stephen, the catholicos or head of the church, and Gregory VII was raised in his place. An unnamed writer carried the Constable Sempad's chronicle on to 1331. He says that in 1322 the king and most of the bishops chose Constantin of Lampron, bishop of Sis, as the next catholicos.

links.note: In July 1054 Cardinal Humbert and two other envoys of the pope cast the patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, out of the church. Their written sentence calls him a patriarch in name only. It says the seeds of heresy are sown among his followers every day. Crusaders took Constantinople in 1204. Pope Innocent III then treated its church as his own. In 1205 he wrote that it had lately come back into unity with Rome.

prose_changes.old: The Maronites take their name from a Syriac monk, Maron, and from the monastery built around his memory. By the medieval period they were a distinct church of the West Syriac liturgical family, concentrated in the mountains and gorges of Lebanon, where their monasteries and hermitages were cut straight into the cliffs. Their early history is unusually hard to recover, because much of what is told about it was written down later and under argument. Specifically over whether the community had once held that Christ had only one will, a position the wider church had rejected. What is clear is that when the crusaders arrived, the Maronites entered into communion with Rome: William of Tyre describes the union around 1182, and in 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti traveled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council, after which a papal bull set out the terms of the union.

prose_changes.old: From the 1140s, church writers in the Rhineland and then in southern France describe communities with their own ministers, their own initiation rite, and a teaching that the visible material world was not the work of the good God. A dualism that placed them outside Christianity as the councils had defined it. In Languedoc they had noble protection and something close to a parallel church, and in 1209 the papacy launched a crusade against them: two decades of war, then inquisition, then the siege of Montségur in 1244, where roughly two hundred of their ministers walked into a fire rather than recant. The last known Languedoc perfect, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. Almost everything known about them comes from the people who destroyed them, and historians now argue seriously about how much of 'Catharism' was a coherent movement at all and how much was a category assembled by inquisitors out of scattered local dissent.

prose_changes.old: Canons regular were clergy who lived in community under a rule — usually the Rule of St Augustine. But who, unlike monks, kept working in the world: serving churches, running hospitals, teaching. The most influential of their houses was the abbey of Saint-Victor on the left bank of Paris, where the master William of Champeaux withdrew from the schools in 1108 and where his successors built a way of learning that refused to choose between the classroom and the cloister.
